main.text: On the ravens that brought Elias bread and meat near the brook Cherith, 1 Reg. XVII, 3.

Now we must speak of Elias, to whom, while he was hiding at the brook Cherith near the Jordan, הערבים, the ravens, at God's command, brought bread and meat twice a day, 1 Reg. XVII, 3. 4. 5. 6. Because this has seemed scarcely credible to captious minds, there are those who deny that ravens are meant by the Hebrew word ערבים orebim. Thus, according to Kimchi, some explain it as merchants, as in Ezech. XXVII, 27., where we have ערבי מערבך, that is, those who trade in your wares. For others ערבים are Arabs, as in 2 Par. XXI, 16. and Nehem. IV, 1. In Bereshith Rabba, ch. 33, we read עיר היא בתחום ביתשאן ושמה ערבו, There is a town named Arabo in the vicinity of Bethshan (or Scythopolis), as Rabbi Judah writes; its citizens are thought to be called הערבים here. For the Arabic translator too, ערבים Orebim are not ravens but the name of a people. For he renders 1 Reg. XVII, 4.: I have commanded لعوربيم [li-ʿwrbym] the Orebimites to feed you. And in verse six: وكان العوربيم [wa-kāna al-ʿwrbym] And it came about that the Orebimites brought him bread and meat ^{(1)}. But it is easy to show that these interpretations have nothing sound in them. For although Ezekiel [II, 807] describes the Tyrian merchants with the periphrasis ערבי מערבך, those who trade in your wares, ערבים by itself nowhere means merchants. Nor would God have said in general terms, I have commanded merchants, but rather I have commanded the merchants of this or that place to feed you. The other renderings are refuted by the location of the place where this miracle occurred. For near the Jordan, where Elias was hiding, there were no Arabs, no Orebimites, nor any town named Arabo, as far as I know. Moreover, Arabs are not called ערבים Orebim in Hebrew, but ערבים Arbim; and as for the town ערבו Arabo, if there ever was one (which is not yet established to my satisfaction), its inhabitants would have been called ערבויים Arabojim ^{(2)}, not Orebim. Furthermore, Elias, ordered to hide there, would not truly have been hidden if the local inhabitants had known of his hiding place. And this hiding place would soon have been disclosed to King Ahab, who was searching for him everywhere with great care ^{(3)}.

Here, therefore, the הערבים are nothing other than true ravens, as, after [col. 215] the Greeks, they are understood by Josephus, the Chaldee, the Syriac, Jerome, most of the Hebrews, and all the Doctors of the Church without exception. God says that he commanded them: I have commanded the ravens (he says) to feed thee there. God is indeed said to command even brute animals, as in 2 Paral. VII, 13. If I command the locust to devour the land. Amos IX, 3. And I will command the serpent, and he shall bite them. And Ion. II, 10. (var. 11.) God spoke to the fish, that it should vomit out Jonah upon the land. But in the same way he commands even inanimate things: the heavens, for instance, Es. XLV, 12.; the clouds, Iob. XXXVIII, 11. Psal. LXXVIII, 23. Es. V, 6.; the dawn, Iob. XXXVIII, 12.; the sword, Amos IX, 4. To command brute animals, or clouds, etc., is to use them to carry out his decrees. Kimchi therefore rightly says here: וטעם צויתי ששמתי בלבם להביא לחם ובשר שתי פעמים ביום, I have commanded (the ravens), that is, I have put it into their mind to bring bread and meat twice a day. But it is in a very different way that he says, in the ninth verse of the same chapter, that he commanded the widow to feed Elias. For he had commanded her either by an express word, or by inclining her mind to charity and piety toward the servant of God. It should further be noted that several ravens, not one, were appointed for this task, as ^{a)} Eutychius of Alexandria holds; for one would not have sufficed to carry the food Elias needed. For in the life of Paul the Hermit by Saint Jerome, among [II, 808] certain other things which I confess I do not understand, there is also this: that a single raven brings a whole loaf, enough for the meal of two men, namely Antony and Paul. They look up, he says, and see that a raven had settled on a branch of the tree, which, flying gently down from there, laid a whole loaf before their astonished faces. After it had gone, Well, said Paul, the Lord has sent us a meal, etc. For sixty years now I have always received a piece of half a loaf; but at your coming Christ has doubled the ration for his soldiers. Here, however, the case is different. For it is not one raven bringing food to several, but several bringing it to one. That food was bread and meat. Many of the ancients hold that these were brought separately: bread in the morning and meat in the evening. Athanasius in the Synopsis: Οἱ κόρακες ἔφερον αὐτῷ, διὰ ῥήματα Κυρίου, πρωΐας μὲν ἄρτους, δείλης δὲ κρέα [Hoi korakes epheron autō, dia rhēmata Kyriou, prōïas men artous, deilēs de krea]. Theodoret on 3 Kings, Question 52: Προσέφερον γὰρ οἱ κόρακες ἄρτους μὲν ἕωθεν, δείλης δὲ κρέα [Prosepheron gar hoi korakes artous men heōthen, deilēs de krea]. Augustine, Sermon 146 De tempore: The raven brought the servant of God bread in the morning, meat in the evening. Eutychius, as cited above: وكان غراب ياتيه في كل يوم بالغداة بخبز وبالعشا بلحم ياكله [wa-kāna ghurāb yaʾtīhi fī kull yawm bi-l-ghadāh bi-khubz wa-bi-l-ʿashā bi-laḥm yaʾkuluhu] And it was a raven that brought him every day bread in the morning and meat in the evening, to eat. This is indeed what the Greek version has in most copies; but the Complutensian has more correctly what is found in the Hebrew, Chaldee, Syriac, Arabic and Roman text: ἄρτους καὶ κρέας τὸ πρωῒ, καὶ ἄρτους καὶ κρέας τὸ δείλης [artous kai kreas to prōi, kai artous kai kreas to deilēs]. For God willed that, amid the utmost scarcity of everything, both bread and meat should be brought to his servant, so that the meal might be complete and his providence in preserving him might shine out the more. To the same purpose is the fact that the ravens brought these meals to the Prophet twice a day, morning and evening, namely dinner and supper, at fixed hours. For that both were customary among the Jews is clear from Luc. XIV, 12. And a midday meal is mentioned in Gen. XLIII, 25. Ruth. II, 14. and Act. X, 9. 10.

The Hebrews in Kimchi anxiously ask where the ravens brought the bread and meat from. Some hold that they were taken from the table of Ahab, others from that of Jehoshaphat. As if the prophet, brought up in the utmost frugality, had needed royal fare. I would rather say that these things were set aside for the prophet by some one of those seven thousand who ^{b)} had not bowed the knee before Baal, whom God [col. 216] willed to be privy to so great a secret. Yet it is safest to answer with the author of the Mirabilia Scripturae, book 2, chapter 15: But whence that raven brought that meat and bread, let him see to it who entrusted it with such a task. Elsewhere ^{c)} an angel of God sets bread and water before this same Elias when he was hungry in the desert, which you will say was more fitting, and Θεοπρεπέστερον [theoprepesteron]. But God also willed the same [II, 809] service to be performed by ravens, to teach that all creatures are subject to his command ^{(4)}. But the raven, you will say, is an unclean bird, defiling everything by its touch. Quite so, since it mostly feeds on carcasses, and the ceremonial law counts it among the unclean birds. But what God has cleansed must not be held unclean, Act. X, 15. The same God who had enacted this law also abrogated it, or at least dispensed Elias from observing it for a time. Although there was no need of such a dispensation. For the observance of ceremonies could be set aside when the necessity of life pressed. Thus Samson was permitted to eat the honeycomb which bees had built in the dead lion, as Theodoret observes on this passage. And David, when hungry, ate without scruple the bread τῆς προθέσεως [tēs protheseōs], which otherwise it was not lawful to eat except for the priests alone, Luc. VI, 4. And accordingly it was rightly decreed that the Jews, when attacked by the enemy on the sabbath day, might fight and repel force with force, 1 Macchab. II, 41. For life was at stake. And the Sabbath is for man, not man for the Sabbath. Marc. II, 27. The author of the Mirabilia asserts that the ravens serving Elias made amends for the fault committed in the flood. The ravens, he says, are commanded to minister to the prophet, so that that bird might be seen to expiate the fault it had committed in the flood, by becoming a faithful servant to Elias, it which had before been negligent and deceitful toward Noah. Chrysostom, in the Sermon On Elias, holds that the Prophet was like the ravens in this: that as the raven is a μισότεκνον [misoteknon] animal, so Elias hated his children, namely the Jews, for their sins, and, having shut heaven by his prayers, had imposed a long famine on them. And that God therefore wished to soften the prophet's mind, exasperated beyond measure, by the example of the ravens, which, harsh and μισότεκνοι [misoteknoi] though they are, yet with a changed disposition now took pity on the prophet and supplied him with food lest he perish of hunger: as if he had said to Elias, Μὴ τοσαύτη παρὰ σοὶ μετὰ Ἰουδαίων μισοτεκνία, ὅση τοῖς κόραξι κατὰ τῶν νεοσσῶν τῶν οἰκείων. ἀλλ᾽ ὅρα νῦν μεταβεβλημένους τοὺς κόρακας. ὅρα τὴν ἐκείνων, ὦ Ἠλία, φιλανθρωπίαν. οἱ περὶ τοὺς οἰκείους ἀπανθρωποὶ νεοσσοὺς, σοῦ γίνονται ξενοδόχοι φιλότιμοι. Ἄτοπόν ἐστιν, ὦ Ἠλία, τοὺς μὲν κόρακας μεσίτας γίνεσθαι πρὸς σὲ τῆς παρ᾽ ἐμοῦ φιλανθρωπίας· σὲ δὲ μεσίτην τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις μὴ γίνεσθαι τῆς παρ᾽ ἐμοῦ κατ᾽ [II, 810] αὐτῶν τιμωρίας. Αἰδέσθητι τὴν τῶν κοράκων μεταβολὴν, καὶ γένου περὶ τοὺς Ἰουδαίους χρηστός. [Mē tosautē para soi meta Ioudaiōn misoteknia, hosē tois koraxi kata tōn neossōn tōn oikeiōn. all᾽ hora nyn metabeblēmenous tous korakas. hora tēn ekeinōn, ō Ēlia, philanthrōpian. hoi peri tous oikeious apanthrōpoi neossous, sou ginontai xenodochoi philotimoi. Atopon estin, ō Ēlia, tous men korakas mesitas ginesthai pros se tēs par᾽ emou philanthrōpias; se de mesitēn tois Ioudaiois mē ginesthai tēs par᾽ emou kat᾽ autōn timōrias. Aidesthēti tēn tōn korakōn metabolēn, kai genou peri tous Ioudaious chrēstos.] Do not hold the Jews, your children, in as great hatred as the ravens hold their chicks. Yet see the ravens now changed. See, O Elias, their kindness. They who are inhuman toward their own chicks show themselves generous hosts toward you. It is absurd, O Elias, that the ravens should be mediators of my kindness toward you, while you do not intercede for the Jews, whom I am punishing. Marvel at the change in the ravens, and be kind toward the Jews. There are some among more recent writers who hold that God the more justly exacted this service from the ravens, that they should feed his prophet, because of the greater care with which he feeds them when, still chicks, they are abandoned by their parents, as they prove from the words of Job, David, and Christ himself, which we have explained otherwise.

The brook Cerith, or Carith, at which this miracle took place, is thought to be the same as the brook Kana, or of the reed-bed, mentioned in Ios. XVI, 8. and XVII, 9. I would readily believe this, and that it was called קנה kana from the abundance of reeds in which Elias lay hidden. Like the one of whom the greatest of poets says,

And the brook כרית Cerith is named from the verb כרה cara, which the Greek translators at Iob. XL, 25. render very aptly by ἐνσιτεῖσθαι [ensiteisthai], that is, to be fed or to eat, because at it the Prophet was miraculously fed by ravens. If this conjecture is true, a prolepsis [col. 217] must be recognized in these words: Hide thyself by the brook Cerith. However that may be, from the sacred text we know this much: that this brook was near the Jordan, and to the east of Samaria. So Josephus was not paying attention when he wrote that Elias withdrew εἰς τὰ πρὸς νότον μέρη [eis ta pros noton merē], to the parts that lie towards the south ^{(5)}. And far more absurdly Eutychius, confusing this retreat of Elias with his forty-day fast on Mount Horeb: وهرب ايلياس النبي علي تخوم الاردن الي جبل حوريب وهو طور سينا وسكن في شعب عين وكان يشرب الما من ذلك الشعب [wa-haraba Īliyās al-nabī ʿalī tukhūm al-Urdunn ilī jabal Ḥūrīb wa-huwa Ṭūr Sīnā wa-sakana fī shiʿb ʿayn wa-kāna yashrabu al-mā min dhālika al-shiʿb] And Elias the prophet fled through the borders of the Jordan to Mount Horeb, which is Mount Sinai, and dwelt by the cleft of a spring, from which he drank water. To these words he adds the rest about the raven bringing bread and meat.

notes.text: To these must be added HERMANN VON DER HARDT, who in a book written in French (Renards de Simson. Machoire d' Ane. Corbeaux d' Elie. Les IV. Monarchies. L'Ante-Christ. Helmstedt 1707, 8vo, p. 41) interprets ערבים as the inhabitants of a certain small town named Oreb, situated by the rock ערב, which is mentioned in Iud. VII, 25.; and this was the same town which Jerome writes was called Araba in his time and formerly Saphorine. This opinion was soundly refuted with many arguments by Reland in Palaestina, p. 914 ff.
Rather ערבנים, just as from שילו, Shiloh, comes שילני, and from Gilo גילני 1 Reg. XI, 29. 2 Sam. XV, 12.

Add to this that the sacred text reports that the prophet lay hidden in that place for the space of a year. Le Clerc did not weigh this; in his commentary on 1 Reg. XVII, 3. he raised certain objections against Bochart, which I omit because they are rather slight. They have also been sufficiently refuted by DEYLING in Observatt. SS. vol. 1, observation 25, p. 129, and by LILIENTHAL in the book he entitled die gute Sache der göttlichen Offenbarung, vol. 5, ch. 10, §§ 161–165, p. 220 ff.

To J. D. Michaelis, in the notes on this passage added to his German translation, it seems probable that Elias snatched from the ravens the birds and smaller wild animals they were carrying to their nests. On this invented opinion let others judge. J. J. HESS tried to recommend it with new arguments, Geschichte der Koenige Iuda und Israel nach der Trennung des Reiches, vol. 1, book 3, ch. 1, p. 98 ff. I have no doubt that the man who committed these things to writing was firmly convinced that bread and meat were brought to Elias by ravens every day. But this whole narrative seems to belong among those which, like many others about the celebrated prophet, were received by word of mouth from ancient tradition and were enlarged and embellished in various ways in the mouths of the people.
But compare what Le Clerc remarked against this opinion on the passage. Reland taught more correctly in Palaestina p. 293.
